title: Get ready for fallout
summary: Before anything happens: pick the shelter spot in each home now, keep water, sealed food and medicine for at least 2 weeks, keep a battery or hand-crank radio, and agree a family plan for being apart. Getting inside is always the best protection (CDC): no pill, mask or product takes its place.

list: In each home your group uses, decide now where you would shelter, by the rules in Where to shelter from fallout.

Go over the plan with everyone so you all know what to do, and give children, older people and anyone with a disability clear instructions on where the shelter spot is (FEMA, Protection in the Nuclear Age, 1985, dated).
Find out the sheltering and evacuation plans of schools, workplaces and care facilities your family uses (Ready.gov), and your community’s plan (CDC).

blocks.p: How long to stay in says that with no word from anyone, plan to keep sheltering “for as long as 2 weeks, and maybe longer (civil defence handbooks, 1968 and 1985, dated).” So keep supplies for at least 2 weeks. FEMA’s 1985 handbook (dated) says the same: have ready at least a two-week stock of water, food and supplies to bring to shelter. Ready.gov’s kit for radiation emergencies includes a spare change of clothes for each family member, a trash bag for contaminated clothing, and sealed food, water and medicine.

list: Water: How much water you need says to store at least 1 gallon (3.8 L) per person per day for 2 weeks. Store it where you will shelter, so nobody has to go out for it.
Food: sealed, non-perishable food, and a manual can opener (Ready.gov). Ready.gov says at least several days; New York State’s kit list says at least 7 days; this app says at least 2 weeks, as above.
Food and drinks that are sealed or were already inside can be used during sheltering (CDC).

blocks.label: How much food to store, and what

blocks.p: Plan toilets that work with the water off, so nobody has to go outside for them (Living in a closed-up house). Keep soap, plastic bags and wipes or cloths for cleaning off after anyone comes in from outside (Ready.gov).

blocks.label: Toilets when the water is off

blocks.p: A closed-up house in a Central New York winter gets cold. Keep a sleeping bag or warm blanket for each person (Ready.gov), warm clothes, and battery CO alarms near where people sleep (Living in a closed-up house). Living in a closed-up house says how to keep warm without flame first, and when anything may burn: never in a sealed room.

blocks.label: Stay warm when the heat is out

list: Keep a battery-powered or hand-crank radio. It keeps working when other ways of getting news fail (Ready.gov). CDC prefers a NOAA weather radio.
If the radio uses batteries, keep extra batteries with it (CDC).
Have several ways to get emergency alerts, including your area’s community alerts and the FEMA app (Ready.gov).
During an emergency, phone calls may be hard to make: try text messages (CDC).
Make a family emergency communication plan (Ready.gov).
Decide where your family will meet if you can’t meet at home (Ready.gov).
Pick an out-of-state contact everyone can tell where they are and how they are (Ready.gov).
Agree now that whoever is where, stays there. Fallout warning says: “Don’t go out to get family: stay where you are (CDC).”
Children and adults in schools, daycares, hospitals and nursing homes will be told to stay inside, and those places have plans to keep them inside (CDC).

blocks.label: Fallout warning: what to do first

blocks.p: The first actions must happen in minutes, so read them before you need them. FEMA’s planning guidance says people should ideally learn how to clean themselves off before an emergency.

blocks.label: Fallout warning: what to do first

list: Potassium iodide (KI): it protects only the thyroid and will not help in a nuclear bomb emergency (CDC). See Potassium iodide.
Table salt, foods with iodine and iodine supplements are not a substitute for KI (CDC).
Hand sanitizer does not protect against radioactive material, and household cleaning wipes should not be used on skin (Ready.gov).
A mask or cloth over your mouth and nose helps cut how much radioactive material you breathe if you must be outside (CDC), but getting inside is always the best protection (CDC).
